letters.title: Inflation is back, and so am I
letters.subject: Inflation is back, and so am I
letters.preview: One chart that explains this week's market, in plain English.
letters.body:
Hi,

It's been a few months since my last email, so first of all, sorry for the silence. From now on I'll send you a short letter every Sunday. One chart, the news that matters for long-term investors, and my honest view, all in plain English.

## Chart of the week

![Monthly change in US consumer prices. Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics.](https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/gggildelgado/nesletter-assets@f0e59f3abf9597afc98013a45a73bcda2dfc1435/charts/2026-11-15.png)

This chart shows how much prices in the US went up each month. The Fed, America's central bank, wants prices to rise about 2% a year. That works out at roughly 0.17% a month, the red line. For three months in a row, prices have risen about twice that fast. That's true even if you leave out food and fuel, which jump around a lot.

## The big story

### Interest rates may go up again

When prices rise too fast, the Fed's main tool is to raise interest rates. Borrowing gets more expensive, people and companies spend a bit less, and over time prices cool down. After the October numbers (BLS, CNBC, 10 Nov), investors now expect a small rise in rates at the Fed's next meeting on 8–9 December (CNBC, Axios).

> **My take:** higher rates usually hurt the most expensive tech companies the most. Investors pay for them today based on profits they expect many years from now, and higher rates make those future profits worth less. If most of a portfolio sits in a few tech names, it's worth knowing that. It is not a reason to panic and sell.

## Two quick ones

- **Chip makers had a bumpy couple of weeks.** The companies that make computer chips fell again on Friday, even though the US stock market as a whole ended the week higher (TheStreet, 14 Nov). Popular sectors swing hard in both directions. That's why I keep each position small.
- **Nvidia reports on Tuesday.** The chip maker shares its quarterly results on 17 November, after the US market closes (Nvidia). It's now so big that its results can move the whole market, so expect big headlines either way.

## One idea

Decide what you'll do when markets fall, before they fall. In the moment, fear makes most of us want to sell. So I wrote my rule down while things were calm: keep investing every month, add a little to the companies I trust most, and avoid anything drastic. It's boring, and that's the point.

Have a good Sunday,
Gonzalo

P.S. I promise this letter will always have fewer acronyms than a Fed press conference. What are you investing for? Retirement, a house, your kids? Just hit reply. I read every answer.
